title: NDT Training in Miami, FL: Aviation NDT, Courses, Costs and Florida Radiography Rules (2026)
metaTitle: NDT Training in Miami, FL — Aviation NDT Courses, Costs & Rules
description: NDT training in Miami: aviation NDT providers like AVI NDT, online courses, costs, SNT-TC-1A and NAS 410 hours, Florida radiographer rules (64E-5) and MRO jobs.
quickAnswer: Miami's NDT market is built around **aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul**. Local provider **AVI NDT** offers NDT training, inspections, procedure development, audits and consulting to aviation and industrial clients [1], and Miami MRO employers hire **NDT Inspector II** technicians who hold ASNT certification or equivalent documented training [2]. Many trainees combine local or online classroom courses [10] with employer on-the-job training. Florida regulates industrial radiography through the **Department of Health, Bureau of Radiation Control**, under Chapter 64E-5 [3][7].

paragraphs: Miami is one of the busiest aviation maintenance centres in the Americas. Airlines, cargo operators and independent MRO shops maintain aircraft, engines and components for customers across Latin America and the Caribbean, and NDT is woven into almost every heavy check and component overhaul. As a result, Miami's NDT jobs lean heavily toward aviation methods and aviation standards.
Training options reflect that. Rather than large college programs, Miami has specialist providers and employer-based training aimed at aviation NDT, supplemented by online courses.

sections.h2: Local training: AVI NDT and specialist providers
paragraphs: AVI NDT is a Miami-based NDT company whose stated purpose is providing NDT services training, inspections, procedure development, audits and consultation to industries including aviation and industrial clients [1]. Providers like this are valuable for trainees because they combine classroom instruction with real-world inspection experience and understand the documentation aviation employers expect.

When comparing providers, ask whether courses are written to NAS 410 as well as SNT-TC-1A, which methods they cover, how many practical hours are included and whether they can document hours in a form your future employer's Level III will accept.

sections.h2: Aviation NDT standards: NAS 410 and employer requirements
paragraphs: Aviation employers typically certify NDT personnel to NAS 410, the aerospace industry standard, under their own written practices and FAA repair-station quality systems. NAS 410 generally requires more classroom and experience hours than SNT-TC-1A for the same method. College programs elsewhere in the country, such as Pima Community College's NDT certificate, now teach courses explicitly aligned to NAS 410 radiographic, ultrasonic and visual methods [9], showing how central that standard has become.

Miami employers advertise accordingly. One NDT Inspector II posting in Miami required a high school diploma, preferred some college, and asked for ASNT NDT certification or equivalent certifiable training with documented classroom and/or OJT experience [2]. Keeping meticulous records of every training hour is therefore essential.

Aviation MRO in Miami relies on eddy current inspection around fasteners, wheels and structures; fluorescent penetrant inspection of engine and landing-gear components; magnetic particle inspection of steel parts; ultrasonic inspection of components and composites; and radiography for internal features. Engine shops add specialized techniques, and composite repair stations need ultrasonic and bond-testing skills.

Beyond aviation, Miami's ports, marine industry, high-rise construction and power plants create demand for weld inspection, ultrasonic thickness testing and visual inspection — useful fallbacks and career extensions for trainees.

sections.h2: Your first year in a Miami MRO shop
paragraphs: A typical first year for a Miami NDT trainee starts on the shop floor of an MRO facility or component repair station. Early tasks include cleaning and preparing parts, running penetrant lines under supervision, assisting with eddy current inspections and recording results in the shop's quality system. Trainees learn quickly that aviation documentation is unforgiving: every inspection must be traceable to the part, the procedure, the equipment and the inspector.

As hours accumulate, employers typically sponsor Level I and then Level II certification in the methods they use most. Second-shift and weekend work is common in busy MRO shops — the Miami Inspector II posting cited above was for a second shift [2] — and flexibility helps trainees get more hours and advance faster.

Miami's role as a gateway to Latin America shapes its aviation industry. Many MRO customers operate aircraft registered across Latin America and the Caribbean, and technicians who speak both English and Spanish can communicate with customer representatives, read documentation in both languages and travel to support work in the region.

For NDT trainees, bilingual skills combined with aviation certifications can open roles in customer support, field service and quality that are harder to fill. Some training providers even offer method courses in Spanish, which can help Spanish-speaking trainees master technical concepts before working in English-language documentation.

sections.h2: Engine shops and composite repair specialties
paragraphs: Within aviation, engine overhaul and composite repair are two specialties with strong demand. Engine shops inspect turbine blades, disks and cases with fluorescent penetrant, eddy current and ultrasonic techniques under strict process controls, while composite repair stations use ultrasonic and bond-testing methods to find disbonds and delamination in flight controls, nacelles and structures.
Trainees who develop expertise in one of these areas, alongside general aviation NDT methods, become valuable to Miami's specialized MRO shops.

Florida regulates radiation sources through the Department of Health's Bureau of Radiation Control under Chapter 404 of the Florida Statutes, implemented through Chapter 64E-5 of the Florida Administrative Code [3][7]. Part IV of 64E-5 covers radiation safety requirements for industrial radiographic operations [3], and the bureau's guidance notes two industrial radiography licence categories, one limited to approved shielded installations and one for broader use [3].

Florida's rules set training, testing, certification and audit requirements for radiographers and assistants; for example, personnel using industrial cabinet X-ray systems must complete 16 hours of training and testing [4]. Outside cabinet systems, a radiographer must be accompanied by at least one other radiographer or radiographer's assistant when working away from a permanent installation, and assistants must work under the personal supervision of a radiographer [5]. A radiation safety officer needs at least one year of documented industrial radiography experience as a radiographer [6], and X-ray registrants must keep inventories, use logs, survey logs and dosimetry records [8].

sections.h2: How NDT certification actually works for Miami trainees
paragraphs: The most common misunderstanding about NDT training is that a school certifies you. In the United States, the documents most employers follow are ASNT's Recommended Practice SNT-TC-1A, the ANSI/ASNT CP-189 standard and the CP-105 topical outlines [18]. Under SNT-TC-1A, certification is employer-based: a school or online course supplies the classroom hours, but your employer's written practice, its Level III and your documented on-the-job experience are what turn training into a certification. Training programs therefore combine formal classroom or online theory with on-the-job training (OJT) performed in a field or lab setting [18].

In practice, a new technician in any city follows the same ladder: complete Level I and then Level II classroom hours for a method, log supervised experience, pass the employer's general, specific and practical examinations and a vision test, and receive Level II certification in that method. Level III — the person who writes procedures, approves techniques and certifies others — requires additional experience and, for most employers, the ASNT NDT Level III examinations.

sections.h2: Training hours you will need by method
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A publishes recommended minimum classroom hours by method and level for high-school-educated candidates [11]. Employers can adopt stricter numbers in their written practice, and aerospace employers working to NAS 410 or customers with their own specifications often do. Visual testing shows the scale of supervised experience involved: SNT-TC-1A recommends 8 training hours for VT Level I and 16 more for Level II, with 70 and 140 hours of experience in the method respectively [12].

sections.h2: Industrial radiography: the extra licensing layer in Miami
paragraphs: Radiography is the one method where federal and state radiation-safety law sits on top of SNT-TC-1A. Under 10 CFR 34.43, a licensee may not let anyone act as a radiographer until the person has received training in the required radiation-safety subjects, completed at least two months of on-the-job training and been certified through a radiographer certification program by a certifying entity [13][14]. ASNT's Industrial Radiography Radiation Safety Personnel (IRRSP) program is one such certifying entity; it combines a computer-based exam with an employer-conducted practical exam and vision check, and many states recognize it [15]. Online radiation-safety courses such as AWS's roughly 40-hour eLearning module can supply the classroom portion, but site-specific training from the employer is still required [16].
In Florida, the Bureau of Radiation Control applies these requirements through Part IV of Chapter 64E-5 [3][4].

Published industry guidance puts classroom training for a single method at roughly USD 600–2,000, with examination fees of roughly USD 200–500 on top [17]. ASNT lists the initial IRRSP combination exam for radioactive-material and X-ray radiography at USD 260 for members and USD 285 for non-members [15]. Longer certificate and associate-degree programs cost more but bundle several methods, labs and job placement support, and community-college options are often eligible for financial aid.

Before paying, ask whether the price includes the practical hours, specimens and exam fees, whether the course is written to SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 or NAS 410, and whether the provider will document your hours in a form an employer's Level III can accept.

sections.h2: How to choose an NDT training provider
paragraphs: Use this checklist to compare schools, online courses and employer programs.
bullets: Training hours that meet or exceed the SNT-TC-1A table for each method and level.
Hands-on labs with real-flaw specimens, not just slides and videos.
Instructors who hold ASNT Level III in the method they teach.
Documentation of hours suitable for an employer's written practice.
A path to OJT — employer partnerships, apprenticeships or placement support.
For radiography, preparation for IRRSP or the state radiographer exam.
Transparent total cost including exams, books and specimens.

paragraphs: NDT's workforce is ageing: the PQNDT salary and benefits survey put the average NDT technician's age at 47 [19]. As experienced technicians retire, employers across energy, aerospace, infrastructure and manufacturing need trained replacements, which is why so many now sponsor training, apprenticeships and on-the-job programs for motivated newcomers.
A route suited to Miami's aviation market:
bullets: Choose a provider offering NAS 410-aligned aviation NDT courses [1].
Start with PT and ET, the workhorses of aviation MRO.
Seek a trainee role at an MRO shop and document every OJT hour [2].
Add UT and MT as your employer requires.
If interested in radiography, learn Florida's 64E-5 Part IV requirements [3][4].
Use bilingual English–Spanish skills as a differentiator with Latin American customers.
Be ready for second-shift and weekend schedules, which help you build hours faster [2].
Keep a meticulous personal training and experience log to match aviation documentation standards.

faqs.q: Where can I get NDT training in Miami?
faqs.a: Local providers such as AVI NDT offer aviation-focused NDT training [1]; online providers cover theory [10], and many Miami MRO employers complete the training with supervised on-the-job hours.

faqs.q: What do Miami NDT employers require?
faqs.a: One Miami Inspector II posting asked for ASNT certification or equivalent certifiable training with documented classroom and/or OJT experience [2].

faqs.q: What standard do aviation employers use for NDT certification?
faqs.a: Most use NAS 410, the aerospace personnel certification standard; some college programs now teach NAS 410-aligned courses [9]. Ask any provider whether its hours meet NAS 410 before you enrol.

faqs.q: Who regulates industrial radiography in Florida?
faqs.a: The Florida Department of Health, Bureau of Radiation Control, under Chapter 64E-5 [3][7].

faqs.q: How much training is required for cabinet X-ray work in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida requires 16 hours of training and testing for personnel using industrial cabinet X-ray systems [4].

faqs.q: Can I work alone as a radiographer in Florida?
faqs.a: Not at field locations — a radiographer must be accompanied by another radiographer or assistant except for cabinet systems [5]. Assistants must also work under the personal supervision of a radiographer when handling sources or equipment [5].
